studies.title: Made In Hardship
studies.meaning: Three oaths, and each is tied to the listener. The city he lives in, his own presence in it, and a parent with a child. Scholars differ over the second line, reading it as saying the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is a lawful resident of Mecca, or that the city's protections would be lifted against him. Then the claim the oaths support: the human being is made in hardship, a word covering both struggle and being made upright.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The city sworn by is Mecca, which had a recognised sanctuary where violence was not permitted, and the surah swears by it while the man addressed is living under threat inside it. The classical sources connect the second ayah to that tension without agreeing on its exact sense. The third oath, a parent and a child, is left unnamed, which the commentators discuss at length.

keyTerms.note: From a root for the liver and for the middle of a thing, and by extension for what is hard and dense. The word carries labour, and the classical readers also hear uprightness in it, a body built to stand.

From the root for untying and for what is released. The ambiguity is why scholars differ: it can mean a person who is settled and free in a place, or one for whom the place's protection has been lifted.
A negative particle attached to the verb of swearing. Grammarians read it as intensifying rather than negating, a formula for a solemn oath, and the same opening is used at the head of other surahs.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was a sanctuary town where blood could not be shed and a hunted man could not be taken. That protection was the town's whole business model, since it made the fairs and the pilgrimage possible. Swearing by that city while its own protections were being bent around one resident put the oath and the situation in the same sentence, and everyone listening knew it.
studies.didYouKnow: The third oath names a parent and a child without naming either, and the classical commentators fill the gap in three ways: the first human and all who came after, Abraham and the son who helped him build the sanctuary, or simply every father and every child. The Quran leaves it open, and the range is preserved rather than resolved.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Hardship is described as the condition of creation rather than as a punishment or an accident. That single move changes what a difficult life means: it is not evidence of disfavour and does not require an explanation. The oaths that precede it are all local and small, a town, a man, a parent, so the largest claim in the passage is grounded in the most ordinary things the listener could see from where he stood.

crossReferences.why: Names what the hardship is for, an ascent the same surah describes a few lines later.
Makes the same claim about human life with a different word, effort that wears a person down.
Records the origin of the sanctuary sworn by here, a prayer for the same city's safety.

studies.applyIt: The next time you catch yourself thinking that life should be easier than this, try the sentence in this ayah as a working assumption for a day: it was made hard on purpose. Notice what stops being an emergency. The claim is not a comfort, but people generally find that expecting difficulty costs less energy than resenting it.

studies.title: The Steep Pass
studies.meaning: A negative statement first: he did not storm the pass. The verb is violent, describing a rush at something steep, and it implies the ascent is taken at speed or not at all. Then the Quran interrupts itself to ask whether the reader knows what the ascent is, and the answer is a short list of concrete acts. None of them is a belief. The first is freeing a person, named by the word for a neck.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah that has just described a man boasting about how much wealth he consumed. Slavery was ordinary in Arabia, and freeing a person was a recognised act of piety that cost real money, since a slave was a capital asset. Hunger years were also recognised, and feeding during one meant giving away what your own household would need. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A verb for throwing yourself at something difficult without hesitating, used of a rider driving a horse into rough ground. It suggests the ascent is not managed carefully but rushed at.
A specific word for a mountain road climbing between rocks, the hard section of a journey. Naming it with the definite article makes it a known place, as though every listener has one.
The idiom uses the word for a neck to mean a person, and the verb means untying. Someone held is pictured as bound at the neck, so freeing them is described as an act done with the hands.
A rare noun for the condition of being hungry, occurring only here in the Quran. It names a day rather than a person, so what is specified is the moment when food is hardest to give away.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A mountain pass outside Mecca was a real thing, not a figure of speech. The routes north climbed between black rock, and a loaded camel took the steep sections slowly while the drivers walked. Everyone knew which passes were hard. Using that word for a moral act told the listener what kind of effort was meant: not sustained walking, but the short stretch where the ground goes up.
studies.didYouKnow: Five ayat in a row here end on the same rhyme, and the words chosen to carry it are unusual ones: the ascent, a neck, hunger, kinship, dust. The rhyme does part of the work, since the list arrives as a single sound repeated, and a listener hearing it once would have carried the whole sequence away.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The steep ascent is defined by actions rather than by states, and the actions chosen have a common feature: each transfers something a person owns to someone who cannot repay. Freedom, food, attention to a relative nobody else is helping. Belief is mentioned in the surah, but after this list rather than before it, which puts the ordering deliberately: the acts are named first and the faith is placed alongside them.

crossReferences.why: Completes the list this unit begins and adds belief and mutual counsel at the end of it.
Gives a longer version of the same list, including the freeing of necks among the acts named.
Shows the same act with the giver's motive attached, and the recipients overlap almost exactly.

studies.applyIt: Look at your own relatives before you look further afield. The ayah specifies an orphan of near kinship, which usually means the person in your family that everyone assumes someone else is handling. Work out who that is, and do one specific thing for them this month: a call, a bill, an afternoon.
